fiscal.text: The government runs a deficit of 8.0% of GDP in 2026 (deficit 7.3% in 2025), with public debt at 128% of GDP. Fiscal policy is expansionary (impulse +0.7 pp of GDP): more spending or lower taxes shift the IS curve right, raising output, interest rates and inflation pressure. High debt limits room for further stimulus and makes the budget sensitive to interest rates.

energy.text: Brent oil is $92 a barrel (+42% in 12 months). The economy is roughly energy self-sufficient (10% of energy use exported on top of home use, 2024). Domestic production cushions the economy, but fuel and transport prices still rise. Rule of thumb: about +1.3 pp on headline inflation. The EIA projects Brent at $75 in 12 months (-18%), so the energy effect on inflation should fade.

islm_text: The policy rate barely moved, so the LM curve stays roughly where it was; changes in output now come mainly from the IS side (fiscal policy, exports, confidence). With a real rate of +0.1% against an assumed neutral of about 0.75%, policy is accommodative: it is still pushing demand up.
currency_text: US rates are -1.13 pp versus the average of the other major central banks. The dollar has barely moved on average against their currencies over 12 months. Because the dollar is the world's reserve currency, Fed moves spill over into every other economy's financing costs and exchange rate. The exchange rate has been fairly stable, so its effect on inflation is small.

inflation.text: Inflation is 3.7%, above target (2%, PCE measure; CPI shown here). Pushing it up: loose real rates, fiscal stimulus, higher oil prices (+42% y/y). Over the next 12–18 months the rules point to inflation rising further above target.
